text: Explain the Document Object Model (DOM) and how the browser constructs the render tree from HTML and CSS.
idealAnswer: The DOM is a hierarchical tree representation of HTML markup parsed into node objects that JavaScript can manipulate. In parallel, the CSSOM is constructed from CSS rules. The browser combines the DOM and CSSOM into a Render Tree containing only visible nodes and computed styles, which proceeds through Layout (geometry calculation) and Painting (pixel rasterization).

conditions.name: DOM and CSSOM Tree Construction
Render Tree Formulation of Visible Elements
Layout Reflow and Paint Rasterization Stages

text: What is the Event Loop in JavaScript, and how do the Call Stack, Microtask Queue, and Macrotask Queue interact?
idealAnswer: JavaScript is single-threaded with a non-blocking concurrency model driven by the Event Loop. Synchronous code executes on the Call Stack. When asynchronous operations resolve, their callbacks are queued: Microtasks (Promises, queueMicrotask) take strict priority and are executed completely before the Event Loop processes the next Macrotask (setTimeout, setInterval, I/O events).

conditions.name: Single-Threaded Call Stack Execution
Microtask Queue Priority (Promises)
Macrotask Queue Scheduling (Timers, I/O)

text: Explain JavaScript closures and lexical scoping with a practical programming example.
idealAnswer: A closure is the combination of a function bundled together with references to its surrounding lexical environment. In JavaScript, inner functions retain access to outer function variables even after the outer function has completed execution and returned from the call stack, enabling private variables, factory functions, and currying.

conditions.name: Lexical Scoping and Scope Chain Definition
Persistent Variable Retention After Execution
Practical Applications (Encapsulation and Currying)

text: What is the Same-Origin Policy (SOP), and how does Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) safely relax it?
idealAnswer: The Same-Origin Policy is a fundamental browser security mechanism that restricts a document or script loaded from one origin from accessing resources on another origin, defined by protocol, domain, and port. CORS is an HTTP-header based protocol where servers specify Access-Control-Allow-Origin headers and handle preflight OPTIONS requests to allow authorized cross-origin requests.

conditions.name: Same-Origin Policy Triple (Protocol, Domain, Port)
CORS Access-Control Response Headers Protocol
Preflight OPTIONS Request Mechanism

text: What is the Virtual DOM in React, and how does the reconciliation diffing algorithm optimize UI rendering?
idealAnswer: The Virtual DOM is a lightweight in-memory JavaScript representation of the actual DOM. When component state changes, React creates a new virtual DOM tree and runs a heuristic O(n) diffing algorithm against the previous tree (reconciliation). It computes the minimal set of changes and batches them to update only the modified real DOM nodes, avoiding costly full-page reflows.

conditions.name: In-Memory JavaScript Representation Concept
Heuristic Reconciliation Diffing Algorithm
Batching and Minimal Real DOM Mutations

text: Compare LocalStorage, SessionStorage, and Cookies regarding storage limits, lifecycle, and security.
idealAnswer: LocalStorage persists ~5-10MB of key-value string data indefinitely until cleared by user or script, accessible only on client. SessionStorage holds ~5MB scoped strictly to the browser tab lifecycle. Cookies store ~4KB, sent automatically on every HTTP request; when configured with HttpOnly, Secure, and SameSite flags, cookies prevent XSS theft and mitigate CSRF.

conditions.name: Storage Capacity and Lifecycle Durability Differences
HTTP Transmission and Header Overhead
Security Attributes (HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite)

text: What is middleware in Express.js, and what is the role of the next() function?
idealAnswer: In Express.js, middleware functions have access to the request (req), response (res), and next middleware function in the application request-response cycle. Middleware executes code, mutates request objects (like parsing JSON or attaching user sessions), and must either send a response or call next() to pass execution to the next handler; omitting next() causes requests to hang indefinitely.

conditions.name: Request-Response Cycle Pipeline Interception
Next() Function and Chain Control Flow
Common Middleware Use Cases (Auth, Logging, Parsing)

text: Explain database normalization and the requirements for First, Second, and Third Normal Forms (1NF, 2NF, 3NF).
idealAnswer: Normalization organizes relational tables to reduce data redundancy and eliminate insertion, update, and deletion anomalies. 1NF requires atomic column values and unique rows. 2NF requires 1NF and that all non-key columns be fully functionally dependent on the primary key (no partial dependencies). 3NF requires 2NF and that no non-key column depends on another non-key column (no transitive dependencies).

conditions.name: Normalization Objectives and Anomaly Prevention
1NF Atomicity and 2NF Partial Dependency Removal
3NF Transitive Dependency Elimination

text: What is HTTP method idempotency, and how does PUT differ from POST and PATCH?
idealAnswer: An HTTP method is idempotent if executing it multiple times with identical parameters yields the exact same server resource state as a single invocation. GET, PUT, and DELETE are idempotent; POST is non-idempotent because repeating it creates multiple subordinate resources. PUT replaces an entire resource representation, while PATCH performs partial updates on specific fields.

conditions.name: Idempotency Definition and Side-Effect Predictability
POST Non-Idempotent Resource Creation
PUT Full Replacement vs PATCH Partial Mutation

text: Explain CSS Box Model and how box-sizing: border-box alters layout sizing calculations.
idealAnswer: The CSS Box Model wraps every HTML element in four concentric areas: Content, Padding, Border, and Margin. Under the default content-box sizing, setting width: 200px specifies only the content width, so adding padding and border increases the rendered box width. Setting box-sizing: border-box includes padding and border within the specified width, simplifying responsive grid layouts.

conditions.name: Four Concentric Box Model Components
Default content-box Dimension Inflation
border-box Containment for Responsive Design

text: How does async/await improve asynchronous code over Promise .then() chains and callback pyramids?
idealAnswer: Promises represent eventual completion or failure of an asynchronous operation, preventing callback hell. Async/await is syntactic sugar built on top of Promises and Generators, allowing developers to write asynchronous non-blocking code that reads sequentially like synchronous code. It enables clean try/catch error handling and avoids deeply nested .then() callback chains.

conditions.name: Callback Hell and Inversion of Control Issues
Promise Chains and Syntactic Sugar Mechanics
Synchronous-Style Try/Catch Error Handling

text: What is component state versus props in modern UI libraries like React or Vue?
idealAnswer: Props (properties) are read-only inputs passed down from parent to child components, enforcing unidirectional data flow. State is an internal mutable data store managed within a component that changes over time in response to user actions or network events. When state updates, the component and its children re-render to reflect the updated data.

conditions.name: Props Read-Only Immutable Parameter Passing
State Internal Mutable Component Memory
Re-rendering Trigger on State Mutations

text: What is Cross-Site Scripting (XSS), and what measures prevent it in modern web applications?
idealAnswer: XSS occurs when malicious JavaScript code is injected into trusted web applications and executed in victims browsers, allowing attackers to steal session cookies, access tokens, or hijack accounts. Defense mechanisms include context-aware HTML escaping, Content Security Policy (CSP) HTTP headers, sanitizing user inputs with DOMPurify, and storing auth tokens in HttpOnly cookies.

conditions.name: XSS Injection and Client Script Execution
Input Sanitization and Context-Aware HTML Escaping
Content Security Policy (CSP) and HttpOnly Defenses

text: What is an N+1 query problem in Object-Relational Mappings (ORMs) and how do you resolve it?
idealAnswer: The N+1 query problem occurs when an ORM executes 1 initial SQL query to fetch N parent records, and then issues N subsequent individual queries to fetch associated child records in a loop, resulting in N+1 database roundtrips. It is resolved using eager loading (SQL JOINs or prefetching with IN clauses) rather than lazy loading child relations individually.

conditions.name: N+1 Query Manifestation and Database Latency
Lazy Loading Anti-pattern Root Cause
Eager Loading with SQL Joins and Prefetching

text: Explain how you optimize database indexing (B-Tree vs Hash) for high-frequency write versus read-heavy analytical workloads.
idealAnswer: B-Tree indexes maintain a balanced sorted hierarchical structure optimal for range scans, sorting, and inequality comparisons with O(log n) complexity, whereas Hash indexes provide O(1) point lookups for exact equality queries but suffer write overhead and cannot serve range scans. For write-heavy workloads, excess indexing must be minimized due to write amplification, while read-heavy analytical workloads benefit from composite indexes and covering indexes.

conditions.name: B-Tree Range Queries and Balanced Tree Ordering
Hash Index Exact Match Point Lookups
Write Amplification and Analytical Workload Trade-offs

text: How do you handle API security, JWT authentication token expiration, and CSRF protection in a distributed web service?
idealAnswer: Secure authentication employs short-lived JWT access tokens with cryptographically signed headers, paired with rotating refresh tokens stored in HttpOnly SameSite cookies to protect against XSS and CSRF token theft. Refresh token rotation invalidates old tokens upon exchange, and token blacklisting via Redis handles immediate revocations in stateless architectures.

conditions.name: Access and Refresh Token Expiration Lifecycle
CSRF and HttpOnly Cookie Hardening
Signature Verification and Distributed Token Revocation

text: Compare Server-Side Rendering (SSR), Client-Side Rendering (CSR), and Static Site Generation (SSG) in terms of SEO, TTFB, and interactivity.
idealAnswer: CSR renders HTML via JavaScript in the browser, providing rich app transitions but suffering poor Time to First Byte (TTFB), slow Largest Contentful Paint (LCP), and SEO indexing issues. SSR generates HTML dynamically on every request on the server, ensuring great SEO and fast initial paint but increasing server compute load and Time to First Byte. SSG pre-renders HTML at build time, offering near-instant TTFB from CDNs and optimal SEO, suited for content that changes infrequently.

conditions.name: CSR Client Execution and First Contentful Paint Bottlenecks
SSR Dynamic Server Execution and TTFB Latency
SSG Build-Time Pre-rendering and CDN Edge Distribution

text: Compare WebSockets, Server-Sent Events (SSE), and HTTP Long-Polling for real-time application updates.
idealAnswer: WebSockets establish a persistent full-duplex TCP connection over port 80/443 after an HTTP upgrade handshake, enabling bidirectional binary/text communication ideal for multiplayer gaming and live chat. Server-Sent Events (SSE) use a standard HTTP connection with text/event-stream headers for efficient unidirectional server-to-client streaming with automatic reconnection, ideal for LLM token streaming. Long-polling repeatedly holds HTTP connections open until updates occur, creating heavy connection overhead.

conditions.name: WebSocket Full-Duplex Bidirectional TCP Protocol
SSE Unidirectional Text/Event-Stream Architecture
HTTP Long-Polling Connection Overhead and Latency

text: Compare Optimistic vs Pessimistic Concurrency Control in relational and document databases.
idealAnswer: Pessimistic locking assumes conflicts are frequent and locks database rows explicitly (e.g. SELECT FOR UPDATE) for the transaction duration, preventing concurrent reads or writes but creating severe lock contention and deadlock risks. Optimistic Concurrency Control (OCC) assumes conflicts are rare, allowing concurrent updates and verifying record version numbers or timestamps at commit time; if the version changed, the transaction rolls back and retries.

conditions.name: Pessimistic Locking Mechanisms and Contention
Optimistic Concurrency Control (OCC) Version Checking
Throughput vs Collision Frequency Architectural Trade-offs

text: How does garbage collection work in V8 (Node.js/Chrome), comparing Generational Scavenging with Mark-Sweep-Compact?
idealAnswer: V8 manages heap memory using Generational Garbage Collection based on the weak generational hypothesis (most objects die young). The heap is split into Young and Old Generations. The Young Generation uses Scavenge (Cheney algorithm), dividing space into From and To spaces and copying live objects during fast minor GC. Objects surviving multiple scavenges are promoted to the Old Generation, which uses Mark-Sweep-Compact major GC to mark reachable objects and compact fragmented memory.

conditions.name: Weak Generational Hypothesis and Heap Partitioning
Scavenge Minor GC with Semi-Space Copying
Mark-Sweep-Compact Major GC and Memory Fragmentation

text: What is an API Gateway pattern, and what responsibilities does it offload from downstream microservices?
idealAnswer: An API Gateway sits as the single reverse proxy entrypoint between external clients and downstream microservices. It offloads cross-cutting concerns including SSL termination, centralized authentication/JWT validation, rate limiting, request routing, API versioning, response caching, and payload transformation, insulating internal service topologies from client coupling.

conditions.name: Single Entrypoint Reverse Proxy Routing
Cross-Cutting Concerns Offloading (Auth, SSL, Rate Limits)
Topology Encapsulation and Payload Aggregation

text: Explain Core Web Vitals (LCP, INP, CLS) and frontend strategies to optimize each metric.
idealAnswer: Core Web Vitals measure real-world user experience: Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) measures loading performance (<2.5s), optimized via image compression, CDN preloading, and critical CSS inlining. Interaction to Next Paint (INP) measures responsiveness (<200ms), optimized by breaking up long tasks, using web workers, and yielding to main thread via requestIdleCallback. Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) measures visual stability (<0.1), optimized by reserving explicit width/height dimensions on images and ads.

conditions.name: LCP Loading Metric Optimization Strategies
INP Responsiveness and Main Thread Task Splitting
CLS Visual Stability and Aspect Ratio Reservation

text: Explain React Hydration, Server Components (RSC), and how they reduce client JavaScript bundle sizes.
idealAnswer: Hydration attaches client-side event listeners to server-rendered HTML DOM nodes, which historically required downloading the entire component JavaScript tree to the browser. React Server Components (RSC) execute exclusively on the server with direct database/filesystem access; their dependencies and component code remain on the server and are serialized into a JSON-like stream, drastically reducing client JS bundle size while preserving client interactivity in leaf Client Components.

conditions.name: Client-Side Hydration and Event Listener Attachment
React Server Components (RSC) Zero-Bundle Execution
Client Components Boundary and Streaming Architecture

text: When designing a MongoDB document schema, how do you decide between embedding sub-documents versus referencing ObjectIds?
idealAnswer: Embedding sub-documents is optimal for 1-to-few relationships where data is accessed together, modified atomically, and bounded in size (e.g. addresses), benefiting from single-document ACID atomicity and eliminating expensive joins. Referencing ObjectIds with $lookup is required for 1-to-many or many-to-many relationships, unbounded collections (e.g. user activity logs), or frequently updated shared entities to prevent exceeding MongoDB 16MB document size limit.

conditions.name: Embedding for 1-to-Few Bounded Atomic Access
Referencing for Unbounded 1-to-Many Collections
MongoDB 16MB Document Limit and Growth Patterns

text: Explain how Node.js utilizes libuv for asynchronous I/O and thread pool offloading.
idealAnswer: Node.js runs single-threaded JavaScript in V8, but offloads asynchronous I/O to libuv. Libuv delegates network sockets directly to operating system kernel event demultiplexers (epoll on Linux, kqueue on macOS, IOCP on Windows) without blocking threads. For operations unsupported by OS async APIs (filesystem I/O, DNS lookups, crypto hashing), libuv dispatches tasks to an internal multi-threaded Worker Pool (default 4 threads, configurable via UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE).

conditions.name: Libuv Architecture and Kernel Event Demultiplexers
Worker Thread Pool for Filesystem and Crypto Tasks
UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE Configuration and Scaling Limits

text: Explain SQL Injection and NoSQL Injection vulnerabilities and how parameterized queries prevent them.
idealAnswer: SQL and NoSQL Injections occur when untrusted user inputs are concatenated directly into database query strings or query objects, allowing attackers to manipulate query logic (e.g. injecting $gt: "" in MongoDB or OR 1=1 in SQL) to bypass authentication or dump data. Parameterized queries and Object Relational/Document Mappings use prepared statements where input data is strictly bound as parameters, ensuring input is treated as literal values, never executable code.

conditions.name: SQL String Concatenation and NoSQL Operator Injections
Parameterized Queries and Prepared Statements Principle
Input Validation and Sanitization Defenses

text: What are the benefits of introducing an asynchronous message queue (e.g. RabbitMQ, BullMQ) into a web backend?
idealAnswer: Introducing a message queue decouples producer and consumer services, moving slow, non-critical background jobs (email dispatch, PDF rendering, video transcoding) out of the synchronous HTTP request-response cycle. It provides traffic smoothing (load leveling) during traffic surges, automatic retry policies with exponential backoff, and dead-letter queues (DLQ) to isolate poisonous messages without failing API requests.

conditions.name: Decoupling and Async HTTP Offloading
Traffic Smoothing and Load Leveling During Spikes
Retry Mechanisms and Dead Letter Queues (DLQ)

text: How does HTTP/2 multiplexing improve performance over HTTP/1.1, and what is Head-of-Line (HoL) blocking?
idealAnswer: HTTP/1.1 requires sequential request-response cycles per TCP connection, suffering from application-layer Head-of-Line (HoL) blocking where slow requests stall subsequent requests, forcing browsers to open up to 6 parallel TCP connections. HTTP/2 introduces a binary framing layer that multiplexes multiple concurrent bi-directional request-response streams over a single TCP connection, eliminating application HoL blocking and providing header compression via HPACK.

conditions.name: HTTP/1.1 Application Head-of-Line Blocking and Multiple Connections
HTTP/2 Binary Framing Layer and Stream Multiplexing
HPACK Header Compression and Server Push

text: Explain Multi-Version Concurrency Control (MVCC) in PostgreSQL and how VACUUM handles dead row tuples.
idealAnswer: PostgreSQL implements MVCC to allow concurrent reads and writes without read-write locking ("readers do not block writers, writers do not block readers"). Every row tuple stores transaction boundaries (xmin for creation txid, xmax for deletion/update txid). When a row is updated, a new physical tuple version is inserted and the old tuple is marked dead. VACUUM scans page blocks to reclaim space occupied by dead tuples whose xmax is older than any active transaction, preventing table bloat and transaction ID wraparound.

conditions.name: Tuple Versioning with xmin and xmax Transaction IDs
Non-Blocking Concurrent Snapshot Isolation
VACUUM Tuple Reclaiming and Transaction ID Wraparound

text: Design an end-to-end Idempotent Payment Processing API that prevents double-charging under network retries.
idealAnswer: An idempotent payment API requires clients to generate a unique UUID v4 Idempotency-Key sent in request headers. The API Gateway or payment service checks an in-memory Redis distributed lock on the key. If an in-flight request exists, subsequent calls return 409 Conflict. If a cached completed payment response exists, it returns the stored response immediately without re-executing. The database uses an atomic transaction with a unique idempotency constraint and two-phase commit with external payment gateways.

conditions.name: Client Idempotency-Key Header and Distributed Locking
Atomic Database Constraints and State Machine Tracking
Cached Response Replaying and Safe Network Retry Protocol

text: Compare HTTP/2 TCP Head-of-Line blocking with HTTP/3 QUIC UDP architecture, detailing 0-RTT handshakes.
idealAnswer: While HTTP/2 multiplexes streams over a single TCP connection, TCP guarantees in-order packet delivery; thus, a single dropped packet stalls all streams on that connection (TCP-level Head-of-Line blocking). HTTP/3 replaces TCP with QUIC built over UDP. QUIC implements independent stream flow control at the transport layer, so dropped packets on one stream do not stall independent streams. QUIC integrates TLS 1.3 encryption directly into transport handshakes, enabling 0-RTT connection resumption.

conditions.name: HTTP/2 TCP Packet Loss Head-of-Line Bottleneck
HTTP/3 QUIC over UDP Independent Stream Transport
TLS 1.3 Integration and 0-RTT Connection Resumption

text: How do you maintain cache-aside consistency with a relational database using write-through, write-behind, and Change Data Capture (CDC)?
idealAnswer: In cache-aside, applications query cache first and populate on miss, but face race conditions when writing. In write-through, writes synchronously update cache and database together. In write-behind (write-back), writes update cache immediately and asynchronously batch flush to database, offering extreme write throughput at the risk of data loss. For high reliability, modern architectures use Change Data Capture (Debezium + Kafka) to tail database transaction logs (WAL) and invalidate or update cache asynchronously with guaranteed ordering.

conditions.name: Cache-Aside Read Miss Pattern and Race Conditions
Write-Through Synchronous vs Write-Behind Asynchronous Flushes
Change Data Capture (CDC) WAL Invalidation Pipelines

text: Explain how modern bundlers (e.g. Vite/Rollup/Webpack) implement Tree Shaking and why ES Modules (ESM) are required.
idealAnswer: Tree shaking is dead-code elimination that removes unused exports from final production bundles. It relies strictly on the static syntax of ES Modules (import/export), where imports cannot be dynamic or conditional at compile time, allowing the compiler to build a deterministic Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) module dependency graph. In contrast, CommonJS (require/module.exports) is dynamic at runtime, preventing static analysis of used exports.

conditions.name: Dead Code Elimination and Bundle Size Optimization
Static Analysis of ES Modules (ESM) vs Dynamic CommonJS
Side Effects Flagging and Pure Annotation Verification

text: Design a distributed WebSocket gateway supporting 500,000 concurrent connections across multiple server nodes.
idealAnswer: A high-scale distributed WebSocket gateway uses an API Gateway / Load Balancer configured with least-connection routing and sticky sessions for initial handshake. Nodes maintain persistent TCP connections in memory, offloading shared state and cross-node pub/sub message broadcast to a clustered Redis Pub/Sub, Kafka, or RabbitMQ broker. Epoll/KQueue non-blocking I/O and horizontal scaling with heartbeat ping/pong keepalive management prevent connection drops and resource exhaustion.

conditions.name: Load Balancing and Sticky Handshake Protocol
Clustered Pub/Sub Bus for Cross-Node Message Routing
Kernel Socket Tuning and Heartbeat Connection Management

text: How do Timing Attacks compromise cryptographic token comparisons, and how does constant-time comparison mitigate them?
idealAnswer: Standard string equality comparisons (like === or strcmp) iterate character-by-character and return early on the first mismatched character. Attackers measure microsecond differences in server response latency to iteratively infer correct secret tokens character by character. Constant-time comparison (e.g. crypto.timingSafeEqual in Node.js) executes the exact same number of bitwise XOR operations across all bytes regardless of mismatches, eliminating timing leakage.

conditions.name: Early-Exit String Equality Comparison Vulnerability
Statistical Timing Variance and Iterative Key Inference
Bitwise Constant-Time Cryptographic Primitives (timingSafeEqual)

text: Explain Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) and ARIES crash recovery protocols in database engines.
idealAnswer: Write-Ahead Logging guarantees ACID durability by appending transaction changes to a sequential log on non-volatile disk before modifying dirty pages in memory or flushing data files. Under the ARIES recovery algorithm, when a crash occurs, the engine executes three sequential phases: Analysis phase (identifies dirty pages and active transactions from the last checkpoint), Redo phase (replays all logged actions forward to restore pre-crash state), and Undo phase (rolls back uncommitted active transactions backwards).

conditions.name: Write-Ahead Log Sequential Disk Durability Invariant
ARIES Recovery Algorithm Three Phases (Analysis, Redo, Undo)
Checkpoints and Compensation Log Records (CLR)
